# Janyris Cotto

Background in IT, networking, graphic & web design, and blockchain. Website: https://janyris.com/

## Cybersecurity projects

- [SOC lab: the legacy server breach](https://github.com/janyris/soc-legacy-server-breach): Incident response on a compromised legacy Linux server in an isolated VirtualBox lab, following PICERL. Found a backdoored FTP service (CVE-2011-2523) and a planted root shell, preserved evidence, contained and hardened the host, and wrote technical and executive reports. Includes a defender's view mapping each stage to MITRE ATT&CK with draft Splunk detections.

## AI in my work

I use Claude and Claude Code every day for research, documentation and scripting. I enjoy working with it, and I verify everything it produces before I rely on it. Long term, I am heading toward AI security.

- [AI-assisted analysis, manually verified](https://github.com/janyris/soc-legacy-server-breach): In the SOC lab I used AI to help plan scans, parse output, research CVEs and draft reports, and I checked every AI-suggested finding with a manual tool before accepting it as evidence.

## Log

- [SOC lab: the legacy server breach](https://janyris.com/#blog/soc-lab-legacy-server-breach) (2026-10-12): A legacy Ubuntu server was flagged for anomalous traffic. In an isolated VirtualBox host-only network, I scanned it from Kali and found about 25 open ports, including vsftpd 2.3.4 with its known backdoor (CVE-2011-2523) and a root shell already listening on port 1524. The scanner could only guess the FTP version because the banner was masked. A targeted script scan confirmed the real version. Taking the guess at face value would have mislabeled the entry point. I captured volatile state before isolating the host, then removed the backdoor, disabled xinetd, firewalled the entry point and verified the ports were closed. I wrote it up as a technical report and an executive briefing. Then I worked the defender's side: for each stage (the scan, the backdoor trigger, the root shell, the persistence) what a SOC would see, where the signal lives, the MITRE ATT&CK technique, and draft Splunk searches to catch it. Validating those against replayed traffic is next.
